Andrew Wiles. Born in 1953, a British mathematician best known for proving Fermat's Last Theorem in 1995, ending a three-hundred-fifty-eight-year quest. His proof, announced in 1993 and corrected in 1995, employed modern machinery: elliptic curves, modular forms, and the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture. Wiles' solution exemplifies how solving old problems often requires new conceptual frameworks, and how persistence—he pursued the theorem for decades—can lead to revolutionary insights spanning fields.

Fermat's Last Theorem states that no three positive integers satisfy a to the n plus b to the n equals c to the n for any n greater than two. Fermat claimed this in 1637, and the claim stood unproven for three hundred fifty-eight years. Wiles proved it in 1993, with a subtle error corrected in 1995, by showing it follows from the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture, now a theorem. His proof uses elliptic curves and modular forms, connecting number theory to complex analysis in unexpected ways.

Wiles developed deep results in deformation theory of Galois representations. This machinery was needed to link elliptic curves and modular forms. His work has applications beyond Fermat. It advances understanding of Diophantine equations, arithmetic geometry, and the structure of numbers.

He became obsessed with Fermat's theorem as a child after reading a popular book. He pursued it for over thirty years. His isolated work on the problem, away from the mainstream, proved fruitful. He avoided the conventional wisdom that the theorem was intractable.

Wiles' proof is one of the twentieth century's greatest mathematical achievements, yet it illustrates a broader truth: old, isolated problems often yield to new frameworks and cross-disciplinary insight. The Taniyama-Shimura conjecture seemed abstract and distant from Fermat until Wiles saw the connection. His work energised arithmetic geometry and inspired a generation of mathematicians. The proof's announcement in 1993 and subsequent correction in 1995 also revealed the human side of mathematics: even great mathematicians make errors, and verification is essential.
